scope: force-field selection methodology for novel polymers

findings.claim: PDMS benchmark of 5 force fields (UA/Frischknecht-Curro, HUANG improved Class II, COMPASS, OPLS-AA, DREIDING) against experimental density/Cp/compressibility/viscosity/thermal conductivity vs temperature. Density RMSE (g/cm3): HUANG 0.0101 (best), OPLS-AA 0.0414, UA 0.0523, DREIDING 0.1337, COMPASS 0.1781 (worst). COMPASS consistently OVERESTIMATED density across the temperature range.
findings.title: Force-Field Benchmark for Polydimethylsiloxane: Density, Heat Capacity, Isothermal Compressibility, Viscosity and Thermal Conductivity
findings.reported_errors: Density RMSE g/cm3: HUANG 0.0101, OPLS-AA 0.0414, UA 0.0523, DREIDING 0.1337, COMPASS 0.1781; COMPASS sign is OVER-prediction, not under-prediction
findings.relevance: Direct multi-FF, same-polymer, same-metric comparison including COMPASS; shows a Class-II field (COMPASS) can be the WORST performer and can err in the opposite direction (over-density) from our measured PCFF under-density, contradicting any assumption that all Class-II fields share PCFF's sign/magnitude of bias

findings.claim: Review of all-atom force fields on PMMA and polyisobutylene (PIB): Class II force fields (PCFF/COMPASS-family) reproduced amorphous density of both polymers within 2% of experiment; OPLS-AA was the only field to keep PIB density error within 2%; GAFF showed discrepancies above 5% for PMMA.
findings.title: A review on all-atom force fields capabilities to predict polymer properties: Case of poly(methyl methacrylate) and polyisobutylene polymer systems
findings.reported_errors: Class II fields: density within 2% for PMMA and PIB (i.e. no systematic large deficit reported for these two polymers); GAFF: >5% error on PMMA density (sign not specified in accessible abstract/snippet); OPLS-AA: within 2% for PIB
findings.relevance: This is a chemistry-adjacent (acrylic, hydrocarbon) literature counterexample: it reports Class II (PCFF-family) density performance WITHIN 2% for PMMA specifically, which is inconsistent in magnitude with our measured PCFF PMMA density deficit of -6.2%. Full text is paywalled beyond the verified abstract/summary, so the exact PCFF-vs-COMPASS split and sign are not confirmed at full resolution.

findings.claim: Atomistic polymer modeling review surveying 82 published MD studies found COMPASS is the most widely used force field for synthetic polymer simulation, followed by OPLS-AA; PCFF was NOT found to be the primary force field used, and PCFF 'has not undergone the same level of continuous refinement and benchmarking as general-purpose force fields, resulting in inaccuracies for some chemistries.' 23 different force fields were used across the 82 studies, with ad-hoc modifications in 27 instances.
findings.title: Atomistic Polymer Modeling: Recent Advances and Challenges in Building and Parametrization Workflows
findings.reported_errors: No single aggregated error table; qualitative finding that PCFF specifically is flagged as under-benchmarked relative to COMPASS/OPLS-AA in the literature
findings.relevance: Corroborates that PCFF is comparatively less validated in the open literature than COMPASS/OPLS-AA — this is consistent with (does not contradict) a possibility that PCFF's polymer-density bias is under-characterized rather than well-established at -5.9%

1_benchmark_studies.synthesis: Multi-force-field, same-polymer benchmark studies exist but are sparse and polymer-specific. Where COMPASS is directly benchmarked against other fields on a single polymer (PDMS), it is not uniformly better than PCFF-family or OPLS-AA — it is reported as the WORST performer among 5 fields tested, and it OVER-predicts rather than under-predicts density. On PMMA/PIB, Class II (PCFF-family) is reported within 2% of experimental density, which is a smaller error than our measured -6.2% PMMA deficit. GAFF is reported to have >5% error on PMMA (same order as our PCFF numbers but a different chemistry-specific case, not a general GAFF-beats-PCFF result).
1_benchmark_studies.gaps: No literature source found that reproduces our exact systematic -5.9% PCFF density deficit across PEEK/PEG/PMMA/PS as a class-wide trend; no study benchmarks COMPASS or GAFF2 against PCFF on PEEK, PEG, or PS specifically (our four chemistries). The PDMS and PMMA/PIB studies are the only same-polymer multi-FF benchmarks found and neither covers our four polymers or corroborates our specific magnitude/sign.

findings.claim: RadonPy (open-source high-throughput MD pipeline for polymer informatics, PoLyInfo-scale, >1000 amorphous polymers, 15 properties) standardizes on GAFF2 for all polymer chemistries. Justification given is GAFF2's broad chemical coverage/established parameterization and automatic bonded/non-bonded assignment via heuristic rules for missing parameters — not a per-polymer field-selection step. The authors explicitly report that GAFF2 density calculation for high-density organic liquids/polymers is 'often poorly performed' and correct this with a machine-learning transfer-learning bias-correction step applied AFTER the raw MD density, rather than by switching force fields.
findings.title: RadonPy: automated physical property calculation using all-atom classical molecular dynamics simulations for polymer informatics
findings.reported_errors: Systematic GAFF2 density bias acknowledged and corrected post hoc via ML/transfer learning rather than resolved by force-field choice
findings.relevance: Directly answers Q2: RadonPy fixes ONE force field (GAFF2) for ALL chemistries rather than doing per-polymer FF selection, and treats a known systematic FF density bias as a statistical correction problem, not a force-field-choice problem. This is a precedent for correcting rather than avoiding a known systematic bias.

findings.claim: A separate GPU-MD high-throughput workflow standardized on the OPLS3e force field and calculated Tg for 315 polymers with experimental values reported, finding 'good agreement' between predicted and experimental Tg across polymer subsets.
findings.title: High-Throughput Molecular Dynamics Simulations and Validation of Thermophysical Properties of Polymers for Various Applications
findings.reported_errors: Qualitative 'good agreement' claimed; no per-polymer quantitative RMSE verified from accessible text (full text paywalled beyond abstract-level claims retrieved via search snippet, not independently WebFetch-confirmed)
findings.relevance: A second precedent for fixing one general-purpose all-atom field (OPLS3e) across an entire cross-chemistry high-throughput screen rather than selecting per-polymer.

2_highthroughput_pipelines.synthesis: The two identified high-throughput pipelines (RadonPy/GAFF2, OPLS3e-workflow) both fix a single force field across all chemistries screened; neither implements automated per-polymer force-field selection. Known systematic bias (RadonPy's GAFF2 density bias) is handled by a statistical/ML bias-correction layer applied after MD, not by switching fields per polymer.
2_highthroughput_pipelines.gaps: No high-throughput pipeline was found that performs automated force-field selection conditioned on polymer chemistry. This means there is no published precedent to cite for a 'pick PCFF vs GAFF2 vs COMPASS per polymer' step — the literature's answer to 'how do pipelines decide' is largely 'they don't decide per-polymer; they pick one field and, if needed, statistically correct its bias.'

findings.claim: 82-study literature survey found no systematic, quantitative relationship established in the literature between a force field's parameterization/training-set coverage and prediction error; instead the dominant practice found was ad-hoc post-hoc parameter modification to match experimental targets, which the authors state causes 'parameter proliferation, loss of transferability, and importantly poor reproducibility' — i.e., the field lacks a standardized error-prediction criterion based on chemical distance from the training set.
findings.title: Atomistic Polymer Modeling: Recent Advances and Challenges in Building and Parametrization Workflows
findings.reported_errors: No quantitative correlation between training-set coverage and error was found reported anywhere in the surveyed literature
findings.relevance: This is the closest published statement to our own measurement that extrapolated-atom-fraction does not predict |error| (our correlations: -0.26 on K, -0.64 on density, i.e. negative, meaning MORE extrapolation associates with LOWER error in our data). The review does not report a quantitative test either way — it reports absence of such a test in the literature, which does not contradict our finding but also does not corroborate it; it corroborates the ABSENCE of an established transferability-predicts-error relationship.

3_transferability_criteria.synthesis: No paper was found that quantitatively tests whether being outside a force field's parameterization set predicts larger simulated-property error, for or against. The one relevant review found states the community relies on ad-hoc post-hoc reparameterization rather than a principled applicability-domain metric, which is itself evidence the field has no validated transferability-predicts-error criterion.
3_transferability_criteria.gaps: No study directly measures or reports a correlation (positive or negative) between atom-type/chemistry extrapolation and property error, so our own negative-correlation finding (-0.26 K, -0.64 density) is neither corroborated nor contradicted by anything found — it appears to be a genuinely novel quantitative result relative to the searched literature.

findings.claim: A modified group-contribution (GAP-based) scheme for Tg prediction, validated on 198 homopolymers, achieved R2=0.9925 (in-sample) with mean relative error 8.09% (96/194 polymers <5% MRE, 87/194 in 5-20% MRE). Reports Bicerano's method at R2=0.9749 on a 320-polymer dataset for comparison (explicitly caveating that R2 values are not strictly comparable across differing datasets).
findings.title: Modified Group Contribution Scheme to Predict the Glass-Transition Temperature of Homopolymers through a Limiting Property Dataset
findings.reported_errors: MRE 8.09% in-sample; ~50% of polymers under 5% MRE; Bicerano comparator R2=0.9749 on a different (320-polymer) dataset
findings.relevance: Direct evidence for Q4a: group-contribution Tg accuracy is roughly 8% MRE in-sample, on ~200 polymers, but validation is in-sample, not out-of-sample/held-out, which is the relevant regime for a truly novel polymer

findings.claim: A hybrid QSPR-GAP method on 146 PAEK-family polymers (77 homopolymers + 69 copolymers) achieved a median out-of-sample RMSE of 8 K for Tg, versus an earlier traditional GAP (van-Krevelen-style) method's in-sample MAE of ~10 K (Weyland et al.), and the authors state traditional GAP methods specifically fail for polymers containing structural fragments absent from the training set.
findings.title: Polymer Informatics Method for Fast and Accurate Prediction of the Glass Transition Temperature from Chemical Structure
findings.reported_errors: median out-of-sample RMSE 8 K (QSPR-GAP) vs ~10 K in-sample MAE for traditional van-Krevelen-type GAP
findings.relevance: Directly on PAEK family (chemically adjacent to our PEEK polymer of interest); confirms group-contribution Tg estimators are usable to roughly +-10 K in this family but that the traditional (non-hybrid) van-Krevelen-style approach specifically degrades for novel fragments — relevant caution for using group contribution as a reference-free check on a genuinely novel polymer

findings.claim: Cohesive-energy-density-derived Hildebrand/Hansen solubility parameters computed via a multi-sample MD procedure with a consistent force field and QM-derived charges achieve RMS accuracy of ~1.1 Hildebrands vs experimental solubility-parameter tables, and the method is proposed explicitly as a discriminating check against experimental/tabulated solubility-parameter data.
findings.title: Hildebrand and Hansen solubility parameters from Molecular Dynamics with applications to electronic nose polymer sensors
fields: general MD/CED methodology, force-field-agnostic method description
findings.reported_errors: RMS ~1.1 Hildebrands vs tabulated experimental solubility parameters
findings.relevance: Direct evidence for Q4b: CED/solubility-parameter comparison against Hansen/Hildebrand group-contribution tables IS used in the literature as an independent MD validation observable, with a reported discriminating accuracy of ~1.1 Hildebrands (roughly a few percent of typical polymer delta values ~15-25 (J/cm3)^0.5)

4_reference_free_validation.synthesis: Group-contribution Tg estimators achieve roughly 8-10 K (or ~5-10% MRE) accuracy against experiment when validated in-sample on 150-320 polymer datasets; true out-of-sample performance on structurally novel fragments is explicitly flagged as a weakness of traditional (van Krevelen/Bicerano-style) group contribution, motivating newer hybrid QSPR-GAP methods. CED/solubility-parameter comparison against Hansen/Hildebrand tables is an established, force-field-agnostic reference-free check with ~1.1 Hildebrand RMS discriminating power, independent of the density/Tg pathway.
4_reference_free_validation.gaps: No literature source gives explicit accuracy numbers for van Krevelen's or Bicerano's ORIGINAL (unmodified) methods on truly out-of-training-set novel polymers — every quantitative accuracy number found is in-sample or on a chemically related family (PAEK), not a genuinely novel/unseen chemistry, which is exactly our use case. No source was found directly comparing CED discrimination power against amorphous-density or Tg discrimination power for judging force-field trustworthiness (i.e., no head-to-head 'CED vs density vs Tg as the most sensitive reference-free check' comparison).

findings.claim: Original COMPASS force field (Sun 1998) validation set spans molecular liquids and molecular crystals across 28 molecular classes, emphasizing small-to-medium molecules; explicit polymer-relevant claim found is PEO: density predicted to accuracy of 1-2% over >=200 K and 180 MPa ranges, with oligomer-to-high-molar-mass PEO extrapolation accurate to better than 1%.
findings.title: COMPASS: An ab Initio Force-Field Optimized for Condensed-Phase Applications-Overview with Details on Alkane and Benzene Compounds
polymers: PEO (explicit polymer case); alkanes/benzene as primary validation focus
findings.reported_errors: PEO density <1-2% error claimed by the original developers
findings.relevance: Confirms original COMPASS validation was primarily on small molecules (alkanes, benzene) with PEO as essentially the sole amorphous-polymer-bulk validation case in the founding paper; broad polymer-family coverage (aromatic/heteroatom-rich polymers like PEEK/polysulfone analogs) is NOT part of the original validation set

findings.claim: COMPASS II (2016) extended COMPASS coverage specifically to 'polymer and drug-like molecule databases' using a fragmentation method to construct small molecules exhibiting key functional groups found in those databases -- i.e. extension is via small-molecule fragments representative of polymer functional groups, not via direct amorphous-bulk polymer density/Tg validation.
findings.title: COMPASS II: extended coverage for polymer and drug-like molecule databases
polymers: fragment-level extension targeting polymer-database functional groups, not amorphous-bulk polymer validation
findings.reported_errors: Not available from accessible abstract-level text
findings.relevance: Clarifies that COMPASS II's 'polymer coverage' claim is atom-type/fragment coverage, not amorphous-bulk density/Tg validation on actual polymer melts -- the same gap our own measurement found (atom-type coverage does not track bulk-property error)

findings.claim: RadonPy (GAFF2 for >1000 amorphous polymers) is the only identified source with amorphous-polymer-bulk (not small-molecule-liquid) validation of GAFF2, and it explicitly reports GAFF2 density is 'often poorly performed' for high-density organic systems, correcting this with post-hoc ML bias correction rather than reporting GAFF2 as inherently accurate on bulk polymer density.
findings.title: RadonPy: automated physical property calculation using all-atom classical molecular dynamics simulations for polymer informatics
findings.reported_errors: Systematic density bias acknowledged, magnitude not isolated by chemistry class in the accessible summary; corrected via transfer learning post-simulation
findings.relevance: Directly answers whether GAFF2 has amorphous-polymer-bulk (not just small-molecule) validation: yes, at scale (>1000 polymers), but with an admitted systematic density bias requiring statistical correction -- GAFF2 is not presented by its own largest-scale users as bias-free on bulk polymer density

5_compass_gaff2_validation_scope.synthesis: COMPASS's foundational validation is predominantly small-molecule-liquid/crystal, with PEO as essentially the sole polymer-bulk case (<1-2% density) in the original paper; COMPASS II's 'polymer' extension is fragment/atom-type coverage of polymer functional groups via small-molecule surrogates, not direct amorphous-bulk density/Tg validation across polymer families. GAFF2's only identified large-scale amorphous-polymer-bulk validation (RadonPy, >1000 polymers) reports and statistically corrects a systematic density bias rather than presenting the field as accurate out of the box. No source was found presenting GAFF2 (or GAFF2_mod) amorphous-bulk validation specifically for aromatic, ring-rich polymer families like PEEK or polysulfone.
5_compass_gaff2_validation_scope.gaps: No polymer-family-resolved density/Tg accuracy table was found for either COMPASS or GAFF2 broken out by chemistry (e.g., aromatic vs aliphatic vs heteroatom-backbone), so no literature basis was found to defend or reject GAFF2 specifically for PEEK/polysulfone-class aromatic backbones as our fallback from PCFF. The claim that GAFF2 is 'defensible for aromatic polymers' is UNSUPPORTED by anything found -- it is a validated small-molecule/aliphatic-heavy force field with an admitted systematic bulk-density bias at the polymer scale, and no aromatic-polymer-specific bulk-density number was located for it.

findings.claim: PCFF's own founding validation paper (Sun 1998, COMPASS) reports a direct, same-conditions comparison between PCFF/CFF91 and COMPASS on benzene and toluene liquid density (NPT, Table 13) and on the NVT pressure predicted at the true experimental density (Table 12). NPT density error vs experiment: benzene COMPASS -1.1%, PCFF/CFF91 -6.3%; toluene COMPASS -1.2%, PCFF/CFF91 -6.5%. NVT excess pressure at the true experimental density: benzene COMPASS +48 bar, PCFF/CFF91 +771 bar; toluene COMPASS -103 bar, PCFF/CFF91 +711 bar. The NVT result gives the mechanism for the NPT result: at the correct density PCFF/CFF91's nonbonded interactions produce far more excess repulsive pressure than COMPASS's, so an NPT barostat relaxes the box to a lower, wrong density to relieve it -- the two tables are the same underlying nonbonded defect viewed from fixed-volume and fixed-pressure ensembles, not two independent observations.
findings.title: COMPASS: An ab Initio Force-Field Optimized for Condensed-Phase Applications-Overview with Details on Alkane and Benzene Compounds
polymers: benzene, toluene (small-molecule liquids, not polymer melts)
findings.reported_errors: NPT density: benzene -6.3% (PCFF/CFF91) vs -1.1% (COMPASS); toluene -6.5% (PCFF/CFF91) vs -1.2% (COMPASS). NVT excess pressure at true density: benzene +771 bar (PCFF/CFF91) vs +48 bar (COMPASS); toluene +711 bar (PCFF/CFF91) vs -103 bar (COMPASS)
findings.relevance: Directly on-chemistry for any aromatic-ring backbone or pendant group (PSTR/PS phenyl, and any other class with a benzene-like ring) -- benzene/toluene are the smallest possible structural analogs of a phenyl-containing repeat unit, and the -6.3%/-6.5% PCFF/CFF91 density errors closely match our own independently measured a-PS (atactic polystyrene, PCFF via EMC, DP=40/10 chains) 300 K density deficits of -6.32% (original equilibration), -5.94% (5->10 anneal cycles), and -5.85% (10ns/10ns widened melt-phase production) -- three separate real runs, two of them deliberately spending extra equilibration compute on different, non-overlapping mechanisms (fixed-volume thermal cycling vs. barostat-active NPT sampling), all converging to within ~0.5 points of the small-molecule benchmark. That convergence across very different compute strategies is itself evidence the deficit is not a sampling/kinetics artifact for this specific system -- see PolyJarvis's own a-PS run history (2026-08-19/20) for the equilibration-time control. NOTE: this is small-molecule liquid evidence extended to a polymer melt by chemical-family analogy, not a direct amorphous-polystyrene-melt benchmark -- no such direct PS PCFF-vs-COMPASS bulk-melt study was found (see gaps in section 1 above).

6_pcff_aromatic_density_mechanism_2026_0.synthesis: PCFF's own 1998 founding paper already documents, on the closest available small-molecule analogs, close to the exact magnitude and sign of density deficit later measured independently on amorphous PS melts in this project. This is chemistry-matched (aromatic-ring) and mechanism-verified (NVT excess-pressure origin of the NPT density shortfall) evidence, which is a stronger form of support than the general cross-polymer COMPASS-vs-PCFF comparisons in section 1 (which are chemistry-mismatched to PS: PDMS is silicone, PMMA/PIB are non-aromatic). It does NOT establish that COMPASS is safe or better for non-aromatic chemistries -- section 1's PDMS finding (COMPASS is the worst of 5 fields tested there, and over-predicts rather than under-predicts) stands as a direct counter-example for a different backbone family and must not be generalized away.
6_pcff_aromatic_density_mechanism_2026_0.gaps: Still no direct amorphous-polystyrene-melt (or any aromatic-backbone polymer melt) PCFF-vs-COMPASS density benchmark in the literature -- the benzene/toluene match is a same-family, not same-polymer, comparison. COMPASS's own EMC integration in this codebase (field_override='compass') has a smaller typing-template vocabulary (96 vs PCFF's 422) and has not been build-tested against PS's actual SMILES as of this writing -- admissibility (ff_capability.py) should be checked before committing equilibration compute to it.

findings.claim: MD study on five novel designed poly(phthalazinone ether sulfone ketone) (PPESK) polymers -- an aromatic ether-sulfone-ketone backbone chemically adjacent to polysulfone/PSFO (shares the diaryl sulfone and diaryl ether linkages) -- used the COMPASS force field (explicitly described by the authors as 'a typical PCFF type force field... proved suitable for polymer and energetic materials') to predict Tg, density, cohesive energy density, solubility parameter, and mechanical moduli (E, K, G, Poisson's ratio) for five newly designed (not previously synthesized) PPESK variants. Predicted Tg values were above 500 K for all five, with the -NH2-substituted variant near 600 K.
findings.title: Molecular dynamics simulation on the physical properties of the novel designed poly-(phthalazinone ether sulfone ketone) (PPESK)
polymers: poly(phthalazinone ether sulfone ketone) (PPESK), 5 novel functionalized variants -- aromatic diaryl-sulfone/diaryl-ether family, closest identified analog to PSFO/polysulfone
findings.reported_errors: No signed percent error vs experiment recoverable from accessible abstract/search-snippet text -- the five simulated PPESK variants are novel designs without prior experimental Tg/density measurements to compare against, so this paper validates COMPASS/PCFF-type internal consistency (CED/solubility-parameter/mechanical-property cross-checks) rather than reporting a simulated-vs-experimental density or Tg error for an existing, measured polysulfone-family polymer
findings.relevance: Weak, tangential evidence: confirms a PCFF-type (COMPASS) field is used in the published literature on the closest identified aromatic diaryl-sulfone/ether-ketone chemical family to PSFO, but because the target polymers are novel (no experimental reference values), this source cannot confirm or deny the sign/magnitude of PolyJarvis's own measured PSFO density deficit (-4.0 to -4.3%) or Tg offset (+2-8%). DOI verified to resolve correctly to this exact article (ScienceDirect PII S0927025618303525) via a doi.org redirect check.

7_psfo_pcff_aromatic_sulfone_2026_08.synthesis: No literature source was found that reports a signed, experiment-referenced density or Tg accuracy number for PCFF/Class-II or COMPASS on polysulfone, polyethersulfone, or a close small-molecule analog (diphenyl sulfone, diphenyl ether sulfone) under the same benzene/toluene-style same-conditions comparison that section 6 found for PS. The one chemically adjacent PCFF-type MD study found (PPESK, aromatic diaryl-sulfone/ether-ketone) uses COMPASS but on novel, experimentally-unmeasured polymer designs, so it cannot corroborate or contradict PolyJarvis's own measured PSFO density deficit (-4.0 to -4.3%, PCFF) or Tg offset (+2-8% vs exp 459-463K). This differs from the PS/section-6 case, where a same-family small-molecule (benzene/toluene) benchmark with an explicit signed error against experiment was available directly from PCFF's own founding paper; no equivalent small-molecule sulfone benchmark (e.g., diphenyl sulfone liquid density under PCFF vs COMPASS) was located despite a dedicated search. PSFO's existing ff_justification_doi (Sun 1994 CFF93 origin paper, 10.1021/ja00086a030) remains a force-field-origin citation, not a class- or chemistry-specific validation, consistent with the existing ff_note in guides/polymer_rules.json ('no class-specific PCFF MD validation paper available yet').
7_psfo_pcff_aromatic_sulfone_2026_08.gaps: Searched: 'PCFF force field polysulfone density MD validation', 'Class II force field diaryl ether sulfone density Tg', 'polysulfone MD COMPASS density Tg', 'bisphenol-A polysulfone MD glass transition', 'diphenyl sulfone/diphenyl ether liquid density COMPASS PCFF benchmark', 'Fried polysulfone MD free volume', 'polyethersulfone COMPASS density Tg'. Found: several polysulfone MD papers (gas-transport/free-volume focus, e.g. 10.1039/d0ra05836j) that do not report force-field density/Tg accuracy vs experiment in accessible text, one Dreiding-forcefield (not PCFF-family) polyethersulfone sub-transition study, and the PPESK COMPASS paper above (novel-polymer, no experimental comparator). No small-molecule diphenyl-sulfone or diphenyl-ether-sulfone liquid-density PCFF-vs-COMPASS benchmark analogous to section 6's benzene/toluene case was found. This is a genuine literature gap, not merely an unsearched one: PSFO/polysulfone appears to remain, in the searched literature, without a chemistry-specific PCFF/Class-II bulk validation, matching the existing polymer_rules.json note.

findings.claim: guides/polymer_rules.json already cites 'PEEK2020' (DOI 10.3390/polym12051054) for PKTN. Independently re-verifying and re-reading this paper's actual content directly (title: 'Combined Molecular Dynamics and DFT Simulation Study of the Molecular and Polymer Properties of a Catechol-Based Cyclic Oligomer of Polyether Ether Ketone', Polymers (Basel) 2020) recovers BOTH a density and a Tg comparison not previously extracted into this file: using the COMPASS II force field on a catechol-based cyclic-oligomer PEEK model, MD-simulated amorphous density = 1.364 g/cm3 vs experimental 1.328 g/cm3 (+2.2%, i.e. COMPASS II OVER-predicts PEEK density, opposite sign from PolyJarvis's PCFF -5.1% under-density); a companion DFT-PBEsol calculation gave 1.395 g/cm3 (+5.1%). MD-simulated Tg = 424.4 +/- 22.3 K (unit cell) / 428.6 +/- 6.6 K (2x2x2 supercell) vs experimental 418.2 K, i.e. about +6 to +10 K (+1.5 to +2.5%).
findings.title: Combined Molecular Dynamics and DFT Simulation Study of the Molecular and Polymer Properties of a Catechol-Based Cyclic Oligomer of Polyether Ether Ketone
findings.relevance: Directly on-chemistry for PKTN (PEEK itself). This is the SAME paper as polymer_rules.json's existing PEEK2020 citation -- the ff_note there records only the Tg figure; this file now also captures its density figure, which is directly comparable to PolyJarvis's own PKTN density measurement. The comparison is stark: COMPASS II OVER-predicts PEEK density by +2.2% in this paper, while PolyJarvis's PCFF measurement UNDER-predicts by -5.1% -- opposite sign and different magnitude, for a related but non-identical Class-II variant (COMPASS II, not PCFF) on a simplified cyclic-oligomer model rather than a full linear amorphous melt. This is informative context, not a same-force-field same-model confirmation or refutation.

8_pktn_pcff_aromatic_ether_ketone_2026_0.synthesis: The one directly-on-chemistry (PEEK) literature source found (already partially cited in polymer_rules.json, now re-read for its density figure as well as its Tg figure) reports COMPASS II OVER-predicting PEEK density by +2.2%, the OPPOSITE SIGN from PolyJarvis's measured PCFF PEEK density deficit of -5.1%. This is a genuine contradiction in direction, not just magnitude, but it compares two different Class-II family members (COMPASS II vs plain PCFF) on two different structural models (a small catechol-based cyclic oligomer vs a full linear amorphous melt), so it cannot be read as disproving PolyJarvis's PCFF-specific finding -- it does, however, undercut any assumption that 'Class-II fields under-predict PEEK density' is a general, force-field-family-wide rule; the sign is evidently model/field-variant-dependent even within the Class-II family, echoing the PDMS COMPASS-over-predicts counter-example already in section 1/6. No literature source was found isolating a density or Tg error specifically for plain PCFF (as opposed to COMPASS II) on PEEK or a linear-melt PEEK model, so PolyJarvis's own internally-reasoned mechanism ('PCFF class-II FF lacks full polarizability corrections for aromatic C=O + ether oxygens') remains unconfirmed and uncontradicted by anything more specific than this cyclic-oligomer COMPASS-II analog.
8_pktn_pcff_aromatic_ether_ketone_2026_0.gaps: Searched: 'PEEK PCFF COMPASS density validation', 'aromatic ether ketone diphenyl ether benzophenone force field density', 'PEEK molecular dynamics density Class II force field experimental', plus the PPESK search from section 7 (aromatic ether-sulfone-ketone family, COMPASS/PCFF-type, but novel polymers with no experimental comparator, not repeated here). No diphenyl-ether or benzophenone (PEEK's small-molecule structural analogs, the role benzene/toluene played for PS in section 6) PCFF-vs-COMPASS liquid-density benchmark was found despite a dedicated search -- this is the same evidentiary gap section 6 flagged as still open for aromatic-ketone/ether chemistries, confirmed to remain open. No source distinguishes plain PCFF from COMPASS II specifically for PEEK density on a full linear amorphous-melt model (as opposed to a small cyclic oligomer).

findings.claim: A 2025 review (already cited in section 1 and in guides/polymer_rules.json for PACR) reports Class II (PCFF/COMPASS-family) force fields reproducing amorphous PMMA density within 2% of experiment, and separately reports GAFF density discrepancies above 5% for PMMA -- both figures are for a SPECIFIC PMMA model configuration, and the review's own framing is a survey of published results, not a single new benchmark run with disclosed tacticity/DP/charge-method metadata visible in the accessible abstract/summary text.

findings.claim: Full-text retrieval of guides/polymer_rules.json's EXISTING PVNL ff_justification_doi paper (previously only its abstract-level claims were on record) recovers detailed, directly-comparable numbers for neat (unplasticized) PVC that were not previously extracted into this file. Using the COMPASS force field (Class II family, same lineage as PCFF) on amorphous atactic PVC (24 repeating units, Mn=25534, built in Materials Studio), the paper reports: Tg by density method = 365.42 K vs experimental 354.15 K (+3.2%); Tg by free-volume method = 363.68 K vs experimental 354.15 K (+2.7%). Elastic-constant-derived (Reuss-averaged Cij) bulk modulus K for pure PVC at 298 K = 2.9470 GPa (decreasing to 1.8160 GPa at 358 K) -- this K value is NOT compared against an experimental reference in the paper (no experimental K/G/E number for neat PVC is cited in the accessible text; only DOP-blend K values are compared relative to each other).
findings.title: Research on the Glass Transition Temperature and Mechanical Properties of Poly(vinyl chloride)/Dioctyl Phthalate (PVC/DOP) Blends by Molecular Dynamics Simulations
findings.reported_errors: Tg: +2.7% to +3.2% vs experiment (COMPASS over-predicts slightly). Bulk modulus K = 2.9470 GPa at 298 K (no experimental K comparator given in the paper itself)
findings.relevance: Directly on-chemistry (PVC itself, not an analog) and the SAME paper already cited as PVNL's ff_justification_doi in guides/polymer_rules.json -- full-text retrieval (via a saved PDF fetch, DOI confirmed to resolve to this exact Springer/CJPS article) surfaces its bulk-modulus number for the first time in this file. This K = 2.9470 GPa (COMPASS) sits almost exactly inside PolyJarvis's own measured PCFF K range (2.7-2.9 GPa) for PVNL -- a striking numerical convergence between two DIFFERENT Class-II-family force fields (COMPASS here, PCFF internally) on the SAME polymer, both landing well below PolyJarvis's cited experimental K band of [3.5,4.5] GPa (this paper does not itself state that experimental band; the comparison is PolyJarvis's own external framing, made here for the first time by juxtaposing the two numbers -- this literature source does not claim a discrepancy vs experiment for K itself). Per the task's explicit guidance, PVC Tg is treated here as informative context only, not as confirming/denying PolyJarvis's own unreliable internal Tg fits: this paper's +2.7-3.2% COMPASS Tg overshoot is a modest, well-behaved result and stands in contrast to (does not resolve) PolyJarvis's internally-flagged PCFF PVC Tg fit pathology.

10_pvnl_pcff_pvc_chlorine_bulk_modulus_2.synthesis: Strong, if partial, CORROBORATION of PolyJarvis's PVNL bulk-modulus underestimate: a full-text-verified, directly-on-chemistry COMPASS (Class II) study of neat PVC reports K = 2.9470 GPa at 298 K, numerically overlapping PolyJarvis's own PCFF-measured K range of 2.7-2.9 GPa almost exactly, for the same polymer under a related but distinct Class-II force field. Because this literature source does not itself state an experimental K value for neat PVC to compare against, it cannot independently confirm that ~2.7-2.95 GPa is too LOW vs experiment -- but the fact that two different Class-II-family force fields (COMPASS and PCFF) converge on nearly the same K value for the same polymer is evidence AGAINST a PCFF-specific numerical artifact and evidence FOR a Class-II-family-wide (not merely PCFF-specific) mechanism underlying PolyJarvis's measured ~20-35% K deficit vs its own cited experimental band -- consistent with, and adding a second independent force field to, PolyJarvis's own robust Murnaghan+fluctuation cross-check finding. No literature source was found that explicitly attributes this to a chlorine/halogen nonbonded-parameter limitation in Class-II force fields specifically (see gaps) -- that specific mechanism hypothesis from Step 2 remains untested by anything found. On density and Tg: this source's PVC density values are only given graphically (Fig. 4, PVC density ~1.28-1.36 g/cm3 over 234-460 K, no explicit 298 K number in text) so no clean density percent-error comparison could be extracted; its Tg (+2.7 to +3.2% COMPASS over-prediction) is informative context only, per Step 2's explicit instruction, since PolyJarvis's own PVC Tg fits are internally judged unreliable and not comparable point-for-point.
10_pvnl_pcff_pvc_chlorine_bulk_modulus_2.gaps: Searched: 'PVC PCFF COMPASS density bulk modulus chlorine parameter accuracy', 'Class II force field chlorine nonbonded halogen limitation', 'PVC bulk modulus MD simulation underestimate force field'. No source was found that specifically identifies a chlorine/halogen nonbonded-parameter deficiency in PCFF or COMPASS (Class II) as a mechanism for underestimating PVC's bulk modulus -- the Sun 1994/1998 Class-II derivation papers address halide ANIONS (alkali-halide salts) not covalently-bound organochlorine parameters, and no dedicated organochlorine Class-II validation paper was found. The K = 2.9470 GPa (COMPASS) figure recovered above was not evaluated by its own authors against an experimental PVC K value, so the corroboration claimed in the synthesis above is an indirect (two-force-fields-agree) argument, not a direct literature-vs-experiment confirmation of PolyJarvis's ~20-35% deficit -- a dedicated experimental-K-referenced Class-II PVC benchmark remains unfound.

findings.claim: A dedicated force-field-comparison study on Viton A (a VDF/HFP 60/40 wt% fluoroelastomer, 66% fluorine -- chemically closest within the PHAL family to PVDF's CF2-CH2 chemistry) computed thermodynamic, structural, and mechanical properties (density, modulus, Tg-region thermal-volumetric behavior) using several atomistic force fields and compared them against available experimental data. Qualitative results recovered from accessible abstract/summary text: OPLS-derived force fields produce more extended, more mobile chains and a SOFTER material (lower modulus) that under-represents molecular structure/packing; other force fields relying on stronger nonbonded interactions interfere with chain dynamics/mechanics; PCFF is reported as most satisfactorily predicting structural properties and thermal-volumetric (density-related) behavior around Tg, showing relatively successful transferability to long-chain architectures.
findings.title: Thermodynamic, structural, and mechanical properties of fluoropolymers from molecular dynamics simulation: Comparison of force fields

fields: others (not individually named in accessible text)
findings.reported_errors: No numeric percent-error values recoverable from accessible abstract/search-snippet text (full text paywalled) -- only the qualitative ranking (PCFF best for structure/density-adjacent Tg behavior; OPLS produces a too-soft, too-extended-chain, under-packed structure) could be confirmed
findings.relevance: Directly cautionary for PHAL's OPLS-AA default: this is a same-family (fluoropolymer), multi-force-field comparison reporting OPLS as producing a systematically too-soft, too-extended-chain structure relative to PCFF and experiment, for a fluoropolymer chemically adjacent to PVDF. This does not itself report a signed density or Tg percent-error for OPLS vs experiment (only a qualitative under-packing/softness finding), so it should be read as a caution flag on OPLS-AA's likely direction of mechanical-property error for PHAL (under-prediction of modulus/stiffness), not as a quantified confirmation. DOI verified to resolve to the correct ScienceDirect article via a doi.org redirect check.

12_phal_oplsaa_fluoropolymer_2026_08.synthesis: The one directly relevant, same-family literature source found provides a QUALITATIVE caution for PHAL's OPLS-AA default: OPLS-derived force fields are reported to produce systematically too-soft, too-extended-chain fluoropolymer structures relative to PCFF and experiment, for a chemistry (Viton A, VDF/HFP) adjacent to PVDF. This does not corroborate or contradict a specific PolyJarvis-measured PHAL number (no internal PHAL density/Tg/K bias numbers were supplied for this task, unlike PSFO/PKTN/PACR/PVNL/PEST), but it is a directionally actionable finding: if PolyJarvis observes a PHAL mechanical-property (modulus/K) under-prediction in future runs, this source offers a specific, named mechanism (OPLS's tendency toward extended, mobile, under-packed chains) worth checking, and identifies PCFF as the literature-favored alternative for fluoropolymer mechanical accuracy specifically -- notably the OPPOSITE of PHAL's own class-default field choice. This adds a new, previously-uncited caution to the existing PHAL ff_note (Watkins & Jorgensen 2001 perfluoroalkane OPLS-AA lineage, Afzal2021 R2=0.87/MAE=20.8K), which did not previously flag any OPLS-AA-specific mechanical-property softness risk.

13_psil_opls_pdms_crossref_2026_08.synthesis: PSIL (PDMS, opls-aa) is the one class in this task's list that ALREADY has a direct, verified, same-polymer multi-force-field benchmark in this file: section 1's finding (DOI 10.1021/acs.jpcb.4c08471, 'Force-Field Benchmark for Polydimethylsiloxane') reports OPLS-AA density RMSE = 0.0414 g/cm3, the SECOND-BEST of five force fields tested (HUANG modified-Class-II best at 0.0101; UA third at 0.0523; DREIDING fourth at 0.1337; COMPASS worst at 0.1781, and COMPASS OVER-predicts). This is already a strong, favorable, same-polymer literature anchor for PSIL's opls-aa default -- among the best-performing of the five fields tested, and not the worst as COMPASS was for the same polymer. This section exists to make that cross-reference explicit for PSIL specifically (the class this file's section 1 finding was not previously tied to by class name) rather than to duplicate it.

findings.claim: A 2023 atomistic-dilatometry study of amorphous cis-1,4-polybutadiene (Mw ~5400 g/mol, LAMMPS) computed specific volume across a temperature/pressure grid using the all-atom pcff+ force field (a PCFF variant -- NOT TraPPE-UA, NOT the PDIE class default), and reports specific-volume deviation of only 2% from experimental data, with a linear Tg-vs-pressure relationship extrapolating to Tg = 162 K at zero pressure and dTg/dP = 0.24 K/MPa.

findings.claim: guides/polymer_rules.json's `ff_justification_doi` field is literally set to Sun 1994 (DOI 10.1021/ja00086a030) on exactly 4 of the 15 _PCFF_CLASSES in mcp-servers/mcp-emc-server/server.py: PCBN, PSTR, PAMD, PSFO (independently re-verified by reading guides/polymer_rules.json directly -- the other 11 PCFF-routed classes, e.g. PKTN/PIMD/POXI/PEST/PSUL/PURT/PANH/PPHS/PACR/PIMN/PVNL, each cite a DIFFERENT, class-specific DOI as their own ff_justification_doi; some of their ff_note PROSE separately mentions 'Sun1994' as general PCFF/CFF93-lineage background, which is a materially weaker, non-citation claim and not a mis-citation). Independently WebFetching and CrossRef-resolving 10.1021/ja00086a030 reveals the paper's ACTUAL title is 'An ab Initio CFF93 All-Atom Force Field for Polycarbonates' (Sun, Mumby, Maple, Hagler, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1994, 116(7), 2978-2987) -- not a generic 'force field for polymers' title as assumed; it is specifically the CFF93 derivation paper for the polycarbonate chemical family. Its own stated methodology (recovered from CrossRef metadata plus corroborating search-engine-indexed secondary-source text, since the ACS abstract page, Wiley, and ResearchGate full text all returned HTTP 403 in this session): force-field parameters were derived by fitting to ab initio (HF/6-31G*) quantum-mechanical total energies, energy derivatives, and electrostatic potentials computed on small MODEL COMPOUNDS representing polycarbonate structural fragments; van der Waals parameters and partial-charge scaling factors were separately fit to CRYSTAL STRUCTURES; resulting molecular-mechanics predictions for the model compounds were compared against experimental values and against the ab initio calculations themselves.
findings.title: An ab Initio CFF93 All-Atom Force Field for Polycarbonates
polymers: polycarbonate model compounds/fragments and crystal structures -- not a full linear amorphous polycarbonate melt, and not PSTR/PAMD/PSFO's own chemistries (the 3 other classes that formally cite this DOI as ff_justification_doi)
fields: CFF93 (direct ancestor of PCFF, Class II lineage)
findings.reported_errors: FULL TEXT independently obtained 2026-08-24 (user-supplied PDF, renamed to literature/Sun_1994_CFF93_FF_Polycarbonates_JACS.pdf, verified against CrossRef's title/authors/journal/year exactly). The paper reports NO liquid, amorphous-melt, or bulk-density/Tg validation of any kind -- its entire quantitative validation is: (1) Table 3, ab initio energy-fit residuals for 5 model compounds (carbonic acid, methyl/dimethyl/phenyl/diphenyl carbonate): RMS total-energy deviation 0.32-0.54 kcal/mol; (2) Tables 1-2, crystal lattice-parameter and lattice-energy comparisons for ethylene carbonate and diphenyl carbonate of 2,2-bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)propane (BPA-PC's carbonate-linked model compound) -- unit-cell edges match experiment to 0.03-0.29 A, lattice energies to 1.1-2.3 kcal/mol; (3) Table 5, dimethyl-carbonate vibrational frequencies vs liquid/vapor IR-Raman spectra, max deviation ~60 cm-1 pre-scaling, close post-scaling; (4) Tables 4/6/7, gas-phase conformational energy differences vs HF/6-31G* and MP2 for dimethyl carbonate, diphenyl carbonate, and 2,2-diphenylpropane (largest deviation ~1 kcal/mol); (5) a single crystal-cluster (7-molecule) ring-flip barrier calculation (~20 kcal/mol, explicitly flagged by the authors themselves as an overestimate due to imposed rigidity). No pure-liquid or amorphous-bulk MD/MC simulation of any polycarbonate, and no density or Tg number of any kind, appears anywhere in the paper.
findings.relevance: This is the formal ff_justification_doi field for exactly 4 PCFF-default classes: PCBN (polycarbonates), PSTR (polystyrenics), PAMD (polyamides), and PSFO (polysulfones) -- independently re-verified by reading guides/polymer_rules.json directly, not merely by narrative cross-reference. The other 11 PCFF-routed classes (PKTN, PIMD, POXI, PEST, PSUL, PURT, PANH, PPHS, PACR, PIMN, PVNL) each cite their OWN, different, class-specific DOI as ff_justification_doi -- only a few of their ff_note fields separately mention 'Sun1994' as informal PCFF/CFF93-lineage background, which is a materially weaker claim (general methodology provenance, not chemistry-specific validation evidence) and not the same finding as a mis-citation. For PCBN specifically this DOI is a genuinely on-chemistry founding citation FOR THE PARAMETERIZATION METHODOLOGY, but full-text reading (2026-08-24) shows it is NOT bulk-property validation even for PCBN: it validates conformational energetics and crystal-lattice structure on small model compounds and dimers only, never an amorphous polycarbonate melt's density or Tg. So PCBN's own PCFF density/Tg accuracy is, on this founding paper's evidence alone, just as unvalidated at the bulk-property level as PSTR/PAMD/PSFO's -- the difference between PCBN and the other 3 classes is chemistry-match, not validation depth. For PSTR/PAMD/PSFO it is being used as a stand-in for 'the PCFF/Class-II force field's founding validation,' when the paper's own actual scope (by its title and its ab initio+crystal-structure model-compound methodology) is the polycarbonate structural family only -- an even narrower scope than the generic 'small molecules' extrapolation already documented for COMPASS in section 5. This paper does not itself claim to validate PCFF broadly across chemistries; that broader claim is an assumption made by this codebase's citation practice on 3 classes, not a statement in the source.

16_pcff_cff91_founding_paper_2026_08.synthesis: This founding paper's own stated scope UNDERCUTS confidence in treating it as validation for the 3 non-polycarbonate classes that formally cite it (PSTR, PAMD, PSFO): its title, methodology (ab initio fitting on polycarbonate-fragment model compounds + crystal-structure-derived van der Waals parameters), and implicit validation set are specific to the polycarbonate chemical family, not a general-purpose 'polymers' derivation. For PCBN itself, it remains a directly on-chemistry, appropriately-scoped citation. For PSTR/PAMD/PSFO, citing this DOI as 'ff_justification_doi' is best read as citing 'the paper that established the CFF93/PCFF Class-II derivation methodology,' not as citing chemistry-specific validation evidence for those 3 classes -- a materially different and much weaker claim than the citation currently implies. This is a real and worth-fixing scope mismatch, though narrower than initially drafted (corrected 2026-08-24: the first pass of this section conflated the formal ff_justification_doi field, set on only 4 classes, with informal 'Sun1994' mentions in ff_note prose across additional classes -- those are lineage background, not a citation claim, and were not mis-scoped). It is not 'small molecules extrapolated to bulk polymers' (the COMPASS/OPLS-AA/TraPPE-UA pattern) but 'one polymer's model compounds cited as founding justification for three unrelated polymer chemistries.'
16_pcff_cff91_founding_paper_2026_08.gaps: RESOLVED 2026-08-24: full text obtained directly (user-supplied PDF, ACS pubs.acs.org watermark confirms legitimate publisher copy) and read in full -- no remaining access gap. The paper's silence on bulk amorphous-melt density/Tg is now a confirmed absence, not an access limitation: the authors' own stated scope (Section 4, 'Molecular Mechanics Calculations and Discussion') never claims or attempts a condensed-phase bulk simulation, only isolated-molecule/crystal/cluster calculations. The genuinely open question this leaves is whether ANY published PCFF/CFF93 study (by these or other authors, on any polycarbonate or other PCFF-routed chemistry) reports amorphous-melt density/Tg validation -- this founding paper itself is confirmed not to be that study, for any of the 4 classes that cite it.

findings.claim: The paper's title, authors (Jorgensen, Maxwell, Tirado-Rives), journal (JACS 118(45), 11225-11236), and 1996 publication date were confirmed via CrossRef DOI resolution. Abstract-level content was recovered from an institutional-repository listing (MD Anderson Cancer Center Elsevier Pure profile, a first-party-adjacent source) and corroborated by search-engine-indexed secondary sources: bonded/torsional parameters were derived by fitting to ab initio (RHF/6-31G*//RHF/6-31G*) rotational energy profiles for more than 50 small organic molecules and ions, achieving average conformational-energy errors under 0.2 kcal/mol vs the ab initio reference; nonbonded (Lennard-Jones + charge) parameters were separately fit and tested via Monte Carlo simulations of 34 PURE ORGANIC LIQUIDS (alkanes, alcohols, ethers, ketones, amides, and similar small-molecule liquid classes), achieving approximately 2% accuracy for both heats of vaporization and densities against experimental values. Bond-stretching and angle-bending parameters were adopted largely from the AMBER all-atom force field rather than independently derived.
findings.title: Development and Testing of the OPLS All-Atom Force Field on Conformational Energetics and Properties of Organic Liquids
polymers: none -- validation set is >50 small organic molecules/ions (torsional fitting) and 34 pure small-molecule organic liquids (nonbonded fitting/testing); no polymer or macromolecule is part of the founding validation set
findings.reported_errors: FULL TEXT independently obtained 2026-08-24 (user-supplied PDF, literature/Jorgensen_1996_OPLS_AA_FF_Organic_Liquids_JACS.pdf, ACS pubs.acs.org watermark) -- prior abstract-level figures confirmed exact. Torsional/conformational energies: average error <0.2 kcal/mol vs ab initio RHF/6-31G* reference, >50 molecules/ions (Tables 1-6). Liquid-phase validation, precise published figures: average error in delta-Hvap = 2.4% (~0.2 kcal/mol), average error in density = 1.6% (~0.02 g/cm3), across 34 pure liquids (Tables 7-10). The 34 liquids include sulfur-containing classes (thiols, sulfides, disulfides -- Table 8/10) but NO fluorine-containing liquid and no siloxane/Si-O liquid of any kind. The paper explicitly states: 'such non-polar and monofunctional systems do not show significant condensed-phase effects on internal energies in going from the gas phase to the pure liquids' -- an explicit scope statement (monofunctional small molecules), not merely a silent omission.
findings.relevance: This is the founding paper behind PHAL and PSIL, the two classes server.py routes to opls/2024/opls-aa (mcp-servers/mcp-emc-server/server.py _OPLS_CLASSES). Its own validation set is entirely small-molecule: gas-phase torsional fitting on discrete organic molecules/ions, and liquid-phase (not polymer-melt) density/heat-of-vaporization fitting on 34 pure small-molecule liquids representing several functional-group classes (alkanes, alcohols, ethers, ketones, amides). Neither PTFE/PVDF/PCTFE-type fluoropolymer chemistry (PHAL) nor siloxane chemistry (PSIL) is a named liquid class among the 34 tested, and polymer/macromolecular bulk simulation is not mentioned anywhere in the recovered abstract-level content. Today's routing of OPLS-AA to whole amorphous PHAL/PSIL melts is therefore an extrapolation beyond this founding paper's own stated validation scope, in the same 'small-molecule founding paper, polymer-bulk application is extrapolation' pattern section 5 already established for COMPASS.

17_oplsaa_founding_paper_2026_08.synthesis: OPLS-AA's own founding paper validates torsional energetics against small-molecule/ion ab initio references and liquid density/heat-of-vaporization against 34 small-molecule organic liquids -- it is silent on polymers entirely. This UNDERCUTS (does not support) treating the paper as direct evidence for PHAL/PSIL bulk-melt accuracy; it establishes that OPLS-AA's nonbonded parameters were tuned to reproduce condensed-phase (liquid) density/cohesive energy for a functional-group-diverse but explicitly small-molecule set, which is a reasonable-but-unverified starting point for polymer melts, not a validated one. Section 12 of this file (PHAL, Viton A fluoroelastomer comparison) already found qualitative literature evidence that OPLS-derived fields tend to produce too-soft, under-packed structures relative to PCFF for a PVDF-adjacent chemistry -- consistent with (not contradicted by) a founding paper whose own validation never tested a fluorine- or silicon-containing repeat unit assembled into a bulk amorphous network. Section 13 (PSIL/PDMS) already found the one favorable same-polymer benchmark (OPLS-AA second-best of five fields) is itself a much later, independent study, not this founding paper.
17_oplsaa_founding_paper_2026_08.gaps: RESOLVED 2026-08-24: full text obtained directly and read in full, including all data tables (7-12) and the explicit-scope sentence quoted above -- no remaining access gap. The paper makes no explicit 'not recommended for X' statement about fluoropolymers, siloxanes, or polymers generally (its Conclusion frames itself as broadly applicable to 'protein dynamics' and future carbohydrate work, not polymers); the PHAL/PSIL gap is a genuine silent omission (no fluorine or Si-O liquid in the 34-liquid set), not a stated exclusion.

findings.claim: The paper's title, authors (Martin, Siepmann), journal (J. Phys. Chem. B 102(14), 2569-2577), and 1998 publication date were confirmed via CrossRef DOI resolution (note the DOI's literal final character is a bare '+', i.e. 10.1021/jp972543+, which resolves correctly when percent-encoded as %2B in a URL). Abstract-level content was recovered directly from the Siepmann research group's own publication listing page (a first-party source): the united-atom Lennard-Jones parameters (a new CH3/CH2 parameter set) were derived and tested via configurational-bias Monte Carlo simulation in the Gibbs ensemble, fitting to critical temperatures and saturated liquid densities of n-ALKANES FROM METHANE THROUGH DODECANE (C1-C12) only. The paper reports that a single CH3/CH2 parameter pair is sufficient to accurately describe fluid-phase behavior across this entire n-alkane range, and explicitly states two limitations: the model does not reproduce experimental second virial coefficients, and saturated vapor pressures/densities show 'small, but systematic' deviations from experimental data. Properties validated: vapor-liquid coexistence curves, critical temperatures, saturated liquid densities, and high-pressure equations of state -- phase-equilibrium properties of small-molecule alkane fluids, not bulk-condensed-phase polymer properties.
findings.title: Transferable Potentials for Phase Equilibria. 1. United-Atom Description of n-Alkanes
polymers: none -- validation set is n-alkanes methane through dodecane (C1-C12), explicitly molecular/oligomeric, not polymeric; no discussion of polymer chain lengths or bulk polymer melts was found in the accessible abstract
findings.reported_errors: FULL TEXT CONFIRMED 2026-08-24 (user-supplied PDF, ACS pubs.acs.org watermark): Table 4 reports liquid density at standard conditions vs experiment with rms deviation 0.0040 g/mL for n-pentane (calc 0.6232, expt 0.6262, ~0.5% low) and 0.0044 g/mL for n-octane (calc 0.7053, expt 0.7025, ~0.4% high); text states densities for octane and dodecane agree with experiment 'to better than 1%.' Table 6 confirms the second-virial-coefficient limitation is a CONSISTENT, SIGNED underestimate of magnitude (10-20% low) across ethane through octane at every temperature tested, attributed explicitly to the LJ parameters being effective (not true) pair potentials fit to reproduce VLCC/density rather than B(T). Table 2 shows normal boiling points systematically underestimated for all three force fields (OPLS/SKS/TraPPE) relative to experiment. No Tg, no bulk/elastic modulus, and no chain length beyond n-dodecane (12 carbons, all fully saturated) appear anywhere in the paper; the longest system simulated (1600-molecule n-octane box, used only for a finite-size check) is still a C8 liquid, not a polymer melt.
findings.relevance: This is the founding paper behind PHYC and PDIE, the two classes server.py routes to trappe-ua (mcp-servers/mcp-emc-server/server.py _TRAPPE_CLASSES). Its own validation set (C1-C12 n-alkanes, phase-equilibrium/critical-point fitting) is the narrowest of the three general-purpose founding papers reviewed in this task -- it is a pure small-molecule/short-oligomer phase-equilibria paper with no polymer-chain-length or bulk-melt discussion at all in the recovered text. Section 14 of this file already independently found that 'the overestimation of characteristic ratios for polyethylene by the TraPPE-UA force field is well-known in the literature' (a structural, chain-conformation caution) even though PHYC's actual polymer-Tg validation (Ramos 2015, section 14) is a SEPARATE, later paper -- this founding paper itself establishes only the small-molecule LJ parameters, with polymer-scale chain-conformational/thermal behavior validated (where it has been validated at all) by downstream papers, not by TraPPE-UA's own 1998 origin paper. PDIE (polydienes, PBD/PI) is chemically even further from n-alkanes (unsaturated backbone, different united-atom typing needed) than PHYC (polyethylene-like), making this founding paper's applicability to PDIE the most extrapolated of any class/founding-paper pairing reviewed in this task.

18_trappeua_founding_paper_2026_08.synthesis: TraPPE-UA's own founding paper validates exclusively against C1-C12 n-alkane phase-equilibrium and critical-point data -- it is entirely silent on polymers, chain lengths beyond dodecane, or bulk condensed-phase (as opposed to vapor-liquid-equilibrium) properties. This is the most narrowly-scoped of the three general-purpose founding papers reviewed (COMPASS/OPLS-AA each covered dozens of small-molecule classes; this covers one homologous series up to C12). It UNDERCUTS confidence in treating the founding paper itself as validation for bulk amorphous PHYC (polyethylene-like) or PDIE (polydiene) melts -- today's usage rests entirely on later, separate downstream validation work (e.g. Ramos 2015 for PE Tg, already cited in section 14) rather than on anything in the 1998 origin paper. The founding paper does, however, directly support the CHOICE of CH3/CH2 nonbonded parameters used in any TraPPE-UA polyethylene-backbone simulation, since those are the exact parameters it derives -- so the mismatch is one of validated PROPERTY SCOPE (phase equilibria of short alkanes vs bulk density/Tg of long polymer melts), not of parameter provenance.
18_trappeua_founding_paper_2026_08.gaps: RESOLVED 2026-08-24: full text obtained directly (user-supplied PDF) and read in full, including all data tables (1-8) and the Concluding Remarks -- no remaining access gap; the group's own abstract-level publication-page summary already recovered in the prior pass is confirmed accurate, not merely first-party-plausible. The paper contains no explicit statement, positive or negative, about transferability to branched, unsaturated, or polymeric chain architectures -- its Concluding Remarks frame the work purely as a three-force-field VLCC/critical-property comparison for linear n-alkanes and note only that a forthcoming second paper in the series 'will describe the extension of the TraPPE force field to branched alkanes.' The genuinely open question this leaves is unchanged: whether ANY later TraPPE-UA paper (this codebase's folder already holds Wick2000 alkenes/alkylbenzenes and Keasler2012 cyclic-alkanes/ethers extensions, both pre-dating this session) reports bulk polymer-melt density/Tg/modulus validation for PE/PP/PIB (PHYC) or PBD/PI (PDIE) -- this founding paper itself is now confirmed not to be that study, for either class.

findings.claim: Full text was retrieved directly from an open-access PDF mirror hosted by the AmberTools/AMBER developers themselves (ambermd.org/antechamber/gaff.pdf), corroborating and extending the abstract-level content already recovered via a Wiley WebFetch of the publisher page. GAFF was designed to be compatible with the existing AMBER force fields for proteins/nucleic acids and to cover 'most organic and pharmaceutical molecules... composed of H, C, N, O, S, P, and halogens.' Three validation tests were reported: (I) structural prediction on 74 crystallographic structures, RMS atomic displacement 0.26 Angstroms, comparable to or better than Tripos 5.2, MMFF94, and CHARMm; (II) hydrogen-bonding energetics on 22 nucleic-acid base pairs, RMS displacement 0.25 Angstroms and RMS relative energy 1.2 kcal/mol vs quantum-mechanical benchmarks; (III) conformational energies on 71 conformational pairs, RMS error ~0.5 kcal/mol vs experimental/QM values. The paper explicitly states known failure modes: parameters are unreliable for 'conjugated/aromatic rings attached to large aliphatic rings,' and atomic partial charges assigned to sulfur and phosphorus 'seem too large.' Polymer or bulk macromolecular simulation is not discussed anywhere in the retrieved full text -- the entire paper is scoped to small, drug-like, and organic molecules, consistent with its stated design goal of automatic parameter assignment for structurally diverse small molecules in a drug-design context.
findings.title: Development and testing of a general amber force field
polymers: none -- validation sets are 74 small-molecule crystal structures, 22 nucleic-acid base pairs, and 71 small-molecule conformational pairs; no polymer or repeat-unit-melt system is part of the founding validation
findings.reported_errors: Structural (Test I): RMSD 0.26 Angstroms across 74 crystal structures. H-bonding (Test II): RMS displacement 0.25 Angstroms, RMS relative energy 1.2 kcal/mol, 22 base pairs. Conformational energies (Test III): RMS error ~0.5 kcal/mol, 71 pairs.
findings.relevance: GAFF is not a class default anywhere in mcp-servers/mcp-emc-server/server.py's routing tables, but is referenced throughout this file as an admissible fallback/comparison field (RadonPy standardizes on GAFF2 for all its >1000-polymer pipeline, sections 2 and 5) and would be the natural candidate if a PCFF/OPLS-AA/TraPPE-UA class needed a fallback for a chemistry outside those three fields' typing coverage. Its own founding paper is explicitly and exclusively small/drug-like-molecule scoped -- crystal structures, base pairs, and conformational pairs, all discrete organic molecules -- with an explicit design intent of automatic parameter assignment for diverse but small molecular structures, not repeat-unit polymer chemistry. This is the clearest of the four founding papers reviewed in this task in stating what it does NOT cover (aromatic rings fused to large aliphatic rings; S/P partial charges) and in being silent on polymers -- RadonPy's own admission (already on record in sections 2 and 5) that GAFF2 density is 'often poorly performed' for high-density organic/polymer systems and requires post-hoc ML correction is fully consistent with a force field whose own founding validation never tested a bulk amorphous polymer melt.

findings.claim: FULL TEXT CONFIRMED 2026-08-24 (user-supplied PDF, AIP Publishing watermark): He, Man, Yang, Lee, Wang, J. Chem. Phys. 153, 114502 (2020), DOI 10.1063/5.0019056. The paper develops ABCG2, a new set of AM1-BCC bond-charge-correction parameters for GAFF2, targeting hydration/solvation free energy (SFE) accuracy rather than density, Tg, or any mechanical property. Original AM1-BCC+GAFF2 gave mean unsigned error (MUE) 1.03 kcal/mol on hydration free energies of 442 neutral organic solutes in TIP3P water, driven by 12 functional-group classes with MUE >1.0 kcal/mol (halogenated aliphatics/aromatics, alcohols, amines, pyrazines/pyridines, nitriles, nitro/nitrooxy compounds, amides, thioethers -- Table I). After re-deriving BCC terms for those groups (ABCG2), MUE across all 442 solutes dropped to 0.37 kcal/mol, with every functional-group MUE at or below 0.6 kcal/mol. ABCG2 was then tested, with no further fitting, on 895 neutral organic solvent-solute pairs (not just water): MUE 0.51 kcal/mol, RMSE 0.65 kcal/mol, Pearson R=0.94 (Table II). The entire paper is an electrostatics/charge-assignment study -- van der Waals and bonded parameters are untouched, and the word 'polymer' does not appear anywhere in the text; every validation system is a discrete small organic solute (27 non-cyclic alkanes up to 8-carbon nitro compounds) dissolved in a single-component solvent box.
findings.title: A fast and high-quality charge model for the next generation general AMBER force field
polymers: none -- validation sets are 442 neutral organic solutes (hydration free energy in TIP3P water) and 895 organic solvent-solute pairs; every system is a single small molecule in a solvent box, not a polymer melt or repeat-unit chain
findings.reported_errors: Original AM1-BCC+GAFF2: MUE 1.03 kcal/mol (442 solutes, hydration free energy, Table I). New ABCG2: MUE 0.37 kcal/mol (same 442 solutes) and MUE 0.51 kcal/mol / RMSE 0.65 kcal/mol (895 solvent-solute pairs across organic solvents, Table II). Both figures are below the paper's stated ~0.6 kcal/mol experimental measurement uncertainty for hydration free energies.
findings.relevance: This is the closest identified 'GAFF2 update' paper matching the task's guidance, and full-text reading confirms it addresses charge assignment specifically (a component of the force field) via solvation-free-energy accuracy, not a comprehensive GAFF2 re-validation across bonded/nonbonded/polymer-scale properties -- it should not be over-read as a GAFF2 polymer-applicability statement. Combined with RadonPy's own admission (sections 2 and 5) that GAFF2 bulk density needs post-hoc correction, this now CONFIRMS rather than merely reinforces the open question of whether any GAFF/GAFF2-family paper (founding or update) directly validates bulk amorphous polymer-melt properties: full-text reading establishes affirmatively that this one does not (no polymer system, no density, no Tg, no modulus anywhere in the paper), closing the access gap without changing the substantive conclusion.

19_gaff_founding_paper_2026_08.synthesis: GAFF's own founding paper is unambiguously and exclusively small/drug-like-molecule scoped (crystal structures, nucleic-acid base pairs, conformational energies of discrete organic molecules), with explicit, named failure modes (fused aromatic/aliphatic ring systems; S/P charge magnitude) that are informative for judging GAFF's/GAFF2's suitability on specific polymer backbones but do not constitute polymer validation. Since GAFF/GAFF2 is not a class default in this codebase's routing (server.py), this founding-paper gap is lower-stakes than the PCFF/OPLS-AA/TraPPE-UA cases, but it directly explains (rather than contradicts) RadonPy's own documented need to post-hoc-correct GAFF2 bulk-polymer density (sections 2 and 5 of this file): the force field's own developers never tested that property or that class of system. The GAFF2-specific charge-model (ABCG2) update paper, now full-text-confirmed (2026-08-24), does not close this gap either -- it substantially improves hydration/solvation free-energy accuracy for small organic solutes (MUE 1.03->0.37 kcal/mol) but is silent on density, Tg, modulus, and polymers throughout; two of two founding/update papers reviewed for the GAFF family are now confirmed, by full text rather than inference, to contain zero bulk-polymer-melt validation.
19_gaff_founding_paper_2026_08.gaps: GAFF's founding paper: full text WAS retrieved (open-access mirror, ambermd.org/antechamber/gaff.pdf) -- this is the strongest access level of the four founding papers reviewed in this task, so the findings above are full-text-confirmed, not abstract-level guesses. GAFF2 charge-update (ABCG2) paper: RESOLVED 2026-08-24, full text obtained directly (user-supplied PDF) and read in full including both data tables and the Conclusion -- no remaining access gap; the prior TLDR-level summary is confirmed accurate and now superseded by the precise MUE/RMSE figures above. No GAFF2-specific COMPREHENSIVE re-validation paper (covering density/Tg/mechanical properties, as opposed to just charges) was searched for beyond this charge-model paper -- if one exists, it remains unlocated in this session; this is the one open item left in this section, not an access limitation.

findings.claim: Wen2020 (the paper formally cited as PIMD's ff_justification_doi) explicitly and verifiably uses PCFF -- WebFetch of the full text confirms: 'All MD simulations were performed using LAMMPS with the PCFF force field.' However, the paper's five simulated polymers are ALL BPADA-based aromatic polyetherimides (4,4'BPADA+MPD [ULTEM], 4,4'BPADA+PPD, 3,3'BPADA+MPD, 4,4'BPADA+CDA, 4,4'BPADA+DDS) -- PMDA-ODA (Kapton), PIMD's own named exemplar chemistry, is NOT among them and is not mentioned in the paper at all.
findings.title: Determination of glass transition temperature of polyimides from atomistic molecular dynamics simulations and machine-learning algorithms
polymers: 4,4'BPADA+DDS -- all aromatic polyetherimides; PMDA-ODA/Kapton NOT studied
findings.reported_errors: Tg (K), MD[rho(T)]/MD[D(T)]/predicted/experimental: BPADA+MPD 525/504/515/490; BPADA+PPD 539/488/499/unknown; BPADA+DDS 542/532/537/520; BPADA+CDA 516/495/551/473; 3,3'BPADA+MPD 524/500/528/511. Density: 'the density of ULTEM from MD simulations is slightly lower than the experimental value, 1.27 g/cm3' (no percent given). None of these five chemistries is PMDA-ODA/Kapton.
findings.relevance: SCOPE MISMATCH for PIMD specifically: this is a verified, on-topic PCFF paper, but for a compositionally different polyimide subfamily (BPADA-based polyetherimides) than PIMD's own named exemplar (PMDA-ODA/Kapton). This is in fact the identical underlying paper legitimately used as PIMN's citation (PIMN's exemplars include polyetherimide/Ultem) -- it validates PIMN's chemistry, not PIMD's.

findings.claim: A 2024 open-access MD study extracts mechanical parameters (Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio) specifically for PMDA-ODA (Kapton) and PMDA-BIA polyimides using the OPLS-AA force field (not PCFF). Simulated Young's modulus for Kapton (2.5 GPa at 4% deformation) is reported to 'almost perfectly replicate' the experimental literature range of 2.5-3.2 GPa.
findings.title: Extraction of Mechanical Parameters via Molecular Dynamics Simulation: Application to Polyimides
findings.reported_errors: Kapton Young's modulus: MD 2.5 GPa vs literature range 2.5-3.2 GPa (within range, near the low end); Poisson's ratio ~0.33, 'within reported values'. PMDA-BIA MD result (~2 GPa) diverged sharply from one cited literature value (Lei et al., 8.5 GPa), leading the authors to question that literature number's reliability rather than their own.
findings.relevance: Confirms PMDA-ODA/Kapton-specific MD literature exists and is accurate for mechanical properties -- but under OPLS-AA, not PCFF. Combined with the Wen2020 finding above, this shows the two axes of PIMD's citation gap are BOTH populated by different papers using different force fields: a PCFF paper that skips PMDA-ODA entirely, and a PMDA-ODA paper that skips PCFF entirely. Neither paper closes the specific gap (PCFF + PMDA-ODA together).

20_pimd_pcff_polyimide_kapton_2026_08.synthesis: Neither CORROBORATES nor CONTRADICTS any specific PolyJarvis PIMD measurement (none exist yet to compare against) -- but the search materially changes what is known about PIMD's citation state. PIMD's formal ff_justification_doi (10.1002/pol.20200050, Wen2020) IS PCFF, verified directly ('All MD simulations were performed using LAMMPS with the PCFF force field'), so PCFF-or-not is answered YES for this DOI. However, the paper covers only BPADA-based polyetherimide chemistries and never touches PMDA-ODA/Kapton, PIMD's own named exemplar -- so despite being a real, verified, on-topic-force-field citation, it is a chemistry-subfamily scope mismatch when attached to PIMD specifically (it is the correct citation for PIMN, not PIMD). This is a new, independently-discovered instance of the same citation-integrity pattern already documented in this file for Sun1994/PCBN (section 16) and now PPHS (section 22, this batch): an on-topic-looking DOI that does not actually validate the class it is formally attached to. A second search located PMDA-ODA-specific MD literature (Rosenauer2024) with strong mechanical-property agreement, but under OPLS-AA, not PCFF -- so a PCFF-validated PMDA-ODA number still does not exist in the literature searched. PIMD's own ff_note ('Sun1994 (CFF93/PCFF) is the FF origin; no class-specific PCFF MD validation paper available yet') is CORROBORATED and reconfirmed by this finding -- the prose note was already honest about the gap. The formal ff_justification_doi field, however, is misleading: it implies (via ff_routing.py's ff_confidence='cited' flag) that a chemistry-specific validation exists for PIMD, when the cited paper's chemistry-specific validation is actually for a different class (PIMN).
20_pimd_pcff_polyimide_kapton_2026_08.gaps: Searched: 'PMDA-ODA Kapton polyimide molecular dynamics PCFF density Tg simulation', general polyimide PCFF searches, and cross-referenced the Wen2020/Rosenauer2024 papers in full. No source combining PCFF (or COMPASS) with PMDA-ODA/Kapton density or Tg vs experiment was found in this search. This is a genuine, actively-searched gap: PIMD (PMDA-ODA/Kapton chemistry) has no PCFF-specific bulk validation in the literature searched, only a PCFF validation of a different polyimide subfamily (BPADA polyetherimides, i.e. PIMN's chemistry) and a non-PCFF (OPLS-AA) validation of the correct chemistry (PMDA-ODA).

findings.claim: Wen2020 explicitly uses PCFF ('All MD simulations were performed using LAMMPS with the PCFF force field') and directly validates PCFF for Ultem (4,4'-BPADA+MPD), matching PIMN's own ff_note claim almost exactly: MD Tg (rho(T) method) = 525 K vs experimental 490 K. The paper computes Tg by TWO independent methods on the same simulation data -- rho(T) (specific-volume break) and D(T) (a self-diffusion-based method) -- and these disagree with each other: rho(T) gives 525 K (+7.1% vs exp) while D(T) gives 504 K (+2.9% vs exp). The paper's own text states: 'results on Tg from the D(T) data are closer to and only about 10 to 20 K different from the experimental Tg,' i.e. the authors themselves flag the D(T) method as more accurate than the rho(T) method already recorded in PolyJarvis's ff_note.
findings.title: Determination of glass transition temperature of polyimides from atomistic molecular dynamics simulations and machine-learning algorithms
findings.reported_errors: ULTEM (BPADA+MPD) Tg K, [rho(T) / D(T) / ML-predicted / experimental]: 525/504/515/490 -- rho(T) error +7.1%, D(T) error +2.9%, ML-predicted error +5.1%. Other four etherimides (no matched experimental Tg for PPD variant): BPADA+DDS 542/532/537/520 (rho +4.2%, D +2.3%); BPADA+CDA 516/495/551/473 (rho +9.1%, D +4.7%); 3,3'BPADA+MPD 524/500/528/511 (rho +2.5%, D -2.2%). Reporting this source under a PANH finding would misrepresent both the force field (custom crystal-adapted, not PCFF-family) and the physical state (crystal/melting-point transition, not bulk amorphous liquid density), mirroring the exclusion logic already applied to the n-hexane paper wrongly nearly attributed to PEST in section 11 of this file -- so it is excluded from findings entirely rather than included with a caveat. A separate search of the drug-delivery/biodegradable-polymer MD literature (the angle this task specifically flagged as worth checking, since polyanhydrides are heavily studied there) surfaced only general statements that COMPASS and PCFF are 'commonly applied' to amorphous solid dispersion (ASD) modeling in pharmaceutical MD generally, with no polyanhydride-specific paper, density figure, or Tg figure recoverable.
